subtopic_detail: CIWA-Ar severity and benzo choice by hepatic function
stem:
A 54-year-old man on a Melbourne inpatient detoxification ward is 16 hours from his last drink. He describes 20 standard drinks per day for six years. Alcoholic cirrhosis was confirmed on biopsy 18 months ago; today his Child-Pugh score is B (9 points) with INR 1.9, bilirubin 55 micromol/L (5-20), albumin 27 g/L (35-50) and mild ascites. He is tremulous and diaphoretic. Nurse-administered CIWA-Ar is 18. He is oriented, has no asterixis, and has no history of withdrawal seizures.

Routine bloods show sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, urea 5.2 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.7-1.1) and glucose 6.4 mmol/L. Thiamine 300 mg IV has been given.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 158/94, RR 20, SpO2 97 percent room air, temp 37.3
data_table.Examination: Tremor of outstretched hands, diaphoretic, alert and oriented, no asterixis, mild ascites
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.9, bilirubin 55, albumin 27, Na 136, K 4.1, creatinine 78, Mg 0.82

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate benzodiazepine choice?

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg PO now, then repeat 2-hourly to CIWA-Ar
options.rationale: Diazepam has active metabolites cleared by hepatic CYP oxidation; in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis this drives oversedation and hepatic encephalopathy. Oxazepam or lorazepam (glucuronidated) is preferred (Source: eTG Addiction).

options.text: Chlordiazepoxide 25 mg PO 4-hourly fixed
options.rationale: Chlordiazepoxide is long-acting and oxidatively metabolised; accumulation in cirrhosis is problematic and it is not on the AU first-line list (Source: AMH).

options.text: Oxazepam 30 mg PO 2-hourly titrated to CIWA-Ar
options.rationale: In significant hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B/C) the recommended benzodiazepines are those metabolised by phase II glucuronidation and lacking active metabolites - oxazepam (or lorazepam). Symptom-triggered dosing to CIWA-Ar is preferred over fixed schedules to reduce cumulative dose. Oxazepam 15-30 mg 2-hourly to a CIWA-Ar target of under 10 is standard (Source: NSW Health D and A Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Midazolam 2 mg IV 2-hourly PRN for this presentation
options.rationale: IV midazolam is short-acting with active hydroxymetabolites; reserved for ICU-level severe withdrawal or delirium tremens, not ward CIWA-guided care (Source: eTG Addiction).

options.text: Clonazepam 1 mg PO 6-hourly fixed in this scenario
options.rationale: Clonazepam is long half-life and hepatically oxidised without a specific role in AU withdrawal protocols; risks accumulation in Child-Pugh B (Source: AMH).

explanation.summary: In alcohol withdrawal complicated by significant hepatic impairment, glucuronidated benzodiazepines without active metabolites (oxazepam, lorazepam) are chosen; symptom-triggered CIWA-Ar-guided dosing is standard.
key_points: Child-Pugh B/C -> oxazepam or lorazepam (glucuronidation)
Preserved hepatic function -> diazepam loading is preferred
Symptom-triggered dosing beats fixed dosing on cumulative dose
Parenteral thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke
Target CIWA-Ar under 10
explanation.pearls: In context: the mnemonic LOT (Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) marks the glucuronidated benzodiazepines safest in liver failure.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Withdrawal seizure vs delirium tremens vs Wernicke's - timing and priority
stem:
A 47-year-old woman is on the general medical ward day 3 after admission for pancreatitis. She drinks 15 standard drinks daily. Overnight she has become progressively confused, tremulous, and visually hallucinating small animals in the corner of the room. She is now oriented only to person, tugging at her lines. Her CIWA-Ar is 26.

She received a single dose of thiamine 100 mg IM on admission and oral diazepam 5 mg twice daily as scheduled prophylaxis; her actual last drink was 68 hours ago. Sodium is 138 mmol/L, glucose 6.1 mmol/L, magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.7-1.1), phosphate normal, ammonia not elevated, and CT brain plain is unremarkable. She has no focal neurology and no ocular palsy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 176/104, RR 24, SpO2 96 percent, temp 38.2
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, diaphoretic, disoriented to time and place, visual hallucinations, no ataxia, no ophthalmoplegia
data_table.Timeline: Last drink 68 hours ago; scheduled diazepam prophylaxis 5 mg BD only
data_table.Investigations: Na 138, glucose 6.1, Mg 0.62, ammonia normal, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase scheduled diazepam to 10 mg QID and reassess in 4 hours in this clinical setting with formal handover documentation
options.rationale: Fixed-dose escalation is too slow for established delirium tremens with CIWA-Ar 26 and haemodynamic instability; symptom-triggered loading with larger diazepam boluses is required (Source: eTG Addiction).

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg IM for the hallucinations in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Antipsychotics do not treat GABAergic withdrawal, lower seizure threshold, and delay definitive benzodiazepine loading; may be added later for persistent agitation once benzodiazepine loaded (Source: eTG Addiction).

options.text: Diazepam 20 mg PO now, repeat 1-2 hourly to CIWA-Ar under 10, plus thiamine 500 mg IV TDS and IV magnesium replacement
options.rationale: This is established delirium tremens (timing 48-96 hours, confusion, hallucinations, autonomic hyperactivity, CIWA-Ar >=20). AU management is aggressive diazepam loading titrated to a CIWA target under 10, with parenteral thiamine at Wernicke-treatment dose 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days given the pancreatitis-driven malnutrition risk and hypomagnesaemia correction because magnesium is a cofactor for thiamine-dependent enzymes and benzodiazepine efficacy (Source: eTG Addiction; NSW Health D and A Withdrawal Guidelines).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Lumbar puncture and empirical IV ceftriaxone for encephalitis in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Timing (day 3, last drink 68 hours), CIWA-Ar 26, autonomic hyperactivity and normal CT plus absence of meningism make CNS infection unlikely; treat withdrawal first (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Phenytoin loading 15 mg/kg IV to prevent progression to seizure in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Phenytoin does not prevent alcohol withdrawal seizures - benzodiazepines do. Phenytoin has a specific indication only if a coexisting seizure disorder is being covered (Source: eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: Delirium tremens emerges 48-96 hours from last drink with autonomic hyperactivity, confusion, hallucinations. Management is aggressive symptom-triggered diazepam loading plus Wernicke-treatment-dose parenteral thiamine and magnesium correction.
key_points: Withdrawal seizure peaks 12-48 h, DTs 48-96 h, Wernicke any time in malnourished
DTs mortality untreated up to 15 percent, treated under 5 percent
Wernicke treatment dose thiamine = 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days
Magnesium is required for benzodiazepine and thiamine action
Antipsychotics adjunctive only, never first-line in DTs
explanation.pearls: In context: any at-risk patient with confusion, ataxia or ophthalmoplegia gets Wernicke-treatment-dose thiamine (500 mg IV TDS) - the prophylactic dose (300 mg IV daily) is inadequate for suspected active Wernicke.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Wernicke's encephalopathy - thiamine dose and route
stem:
A 61-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after being found confused in a park. He is known to drink one to two litres of cask wine per day and lives in supported accommodation. On arrival he is disoriented to time and place, has horizontal nystagmus and a broad-based unsteady gait. He does not smell of recent alcohol. He has not eaten for at least two days.

Capillary glucose is 3.9 mmol/L. Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, magnesium 0.68 mmol/L (0.7-1.1). CT brain is unremarkable. Ammonia is not elevated. He has no focal weakness and no signs of head trauma.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 128/78, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.6
data_table.Examination: Horizontal nystagmus, broad-based ataxia, disoriented to time and place, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: BSL 3.9, Na 138, K 3.7, Mg 0.68, ammonia normal, CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Thiamine 100 mg IM daily for 3 days then oral 100 mg daily in this clinical setting
options.rationale: 100 mg IM is a prophylactic-only dose; a patient with the Wernicke triad requires the Wernicke-treatment dose (500 mg IV TDS x 2-3 days) which produces substantially higher CSF concentrations (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Thiamine 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days, then reassess for step-down to 300 mg IV daily
options.rationale: The triad of confusion, ophthalmoplegia (nystagmus counts) and ataxia is presumed Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise. AU guidance is high-dose parenteral thiamine 500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days, then step-down to 300 mg IV daily for a further 3-5 days, then oral 100 mg TDS. Magnesium is a cofactor and should be corrected. Any carbohydrate load must follow, not precede, thiamine (Source: eTG Neurology; RANZCP Wernicke position statement).

options.text: IV 50 percent dextrose 50 mL first, then oral thiamine 100 mg for this presentation
options.rationale: Administering carbohydrate before parenteral thiamine in a thiamine-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy; thiamine must precede glucose (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Oral thiamine 300 mg daily with folate and B12 co-administration under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Oral thiamine is poorly absorbed in this population and inadequate for suspected acute Wernicke; parenteral route is required initially (Source: eTG Neurology).

options.text: Diazepam 10 mg IV for suspected complex partial seizure in this clinical setting
options.rationale: The clinical picture is not a seizure; benzodiazepines do not treat Wernicke and delay definitive thiamine (Source: eTG Neurology).

explanation.summary: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy needs high-dose parenteral thiamine (500 mg IV TDS for 2-3 days), given before any carbohydrate load. Magnesium is a required cofactor and should be corrected.
key_points: Classical triad: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia (all three in only 10 percent)
Treatment dose: 500 mg IV TDS x 2-3 days
Prophylactic dose (300 mg IV daily) is not enough for active Wernicke
Thiamine before glucose (glucose-first can precipitate Wernicke)
Magnesium is a thiamine-enzyme cofactor - correct alongside
explanation.pearls: In context: any at-risk patient with even one Wernicke feature earns treatment-dose thiamine; the diagnosis is clinical and treatment cannot wait for MRI.

subtopic_detail: MATOD selection: methadone vs buprenorphine vs buprenorphine-naloxone
stem:
A 34-year-old man attends a public opioid treatment program (OTP) clinic in Sydney requesting to start medication-assisted treatment. He injects heroin daily (approximately 0.5 g), has never been on maintenance treatment before, and has a two-year history of injecting via femoral access. He works full-time in construction, drives 45 minutes to work each morning, and lives with his partner and two young children. He wants a regimen that allows unsupervised take-away doses at the earliest safe opportunity to minimise clinic attendance.

He has no cardiac history and a recent ECG shows QTc 420 ms. LFTs are within normal limits. Urine drug screen is positive for morphine and codeine and negative for benzodiazepines, methamphetamine and cocaine. He is not on any other CNS depressants and reports no alcohol use.

data_table.History: Daily IV heroin 0.5 g, 2 years IVDU, no prior MATOD, working full-time
data_table.Family: Lives with partner and two children aged 3 and 5
data_table.Investigations: ECG QTc 420 ms, LFTs normal, UDS heroin metabolites positive, benzos/meth/cocaine negative
data_table.Preferences: Wants earliest safe take-away doses to reduce clinic attendance

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line MATOD choice?

options.text: Methadone syrup 30 mg PO daily supervised in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Methadone requires prolonged supervised dosing (typically 3+ months of stability) before take-aways, and QT-prolonging risk profile is less favourable here. Buprenorphine-naloxone has a better take-away trajectory in a young worker with children in the home (Source: RACGP MATOD; National Guidelines for MATOD).

options.text: Buprenorphine mono-product 4 mg SL day 1 titrated in this scenario
options.rationale: Mono-product buprenorphine is reserved for pregnancy or documented naloxone hypersensitivity; naloxone-combined product is preferred to reduce injection diversion, especially with children in the home (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

options.text: Buprenorphine-naloxone 4 mg/1 mg SL day 1, titrate up
options.rationale: Buprenorphine-naloxone is preferred first-line in the setting of a young worker who wants early take-aways, has children in the home (naloxone reduces IV diversion risk), and has no contraindication. The National Guidelines for MATOD support quicker take-away schedules on buprenorphine-naloxone than on methadone. Start day 1 dose 4 mg after objective withdrawal has begun (COWS >=12) to reduce precipitated-withdrawal risk (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RACGP).

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily after supervised opioid detox
options.rationale: Oral naltrexone has poor adherence and high overdose-on-relapse risk after detox; not first-line in daily heroin dependence per AU guidelines (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

options.text: Long-acting injectable buprenorphine (Buvidal) 8 mg SC weekly loading
options.rationale: Depot buprenorphine is a reasonable option but AU practice usually stabilises on sublingual buprenorphine-naloxone first before conversion to depot; loading straight to depot in a treatment-naive patient risks precipitated withdrawal management complexity (Source: RACGP MATOD).

explanation.summary: In treatment-naive opioid use disorder without contraindications, buprenorphine-naloxone is first-line where early take-aways are needed and where children in the home make diversion prevention important. Methadone is favoured when higher potency, sedation, or full-agonist coverage is needed (severe dependence, existing methadone tolerance, pregnancy is a nuanced discussion).
key_points: Buprenorphine-naloxone: safer overdose profile, faster take-away schedule
Methadone: full agonist, longer supervised phase, QT and interaction risk
Mono-buprenorphine indications: pregnancy, naloxone hypersensitivity
Depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) after SL stabilisation typically
Confirm objective withdrawal (COWS >=12) before first buprenorphine dose
explanation.pearls: In context: PBS Section 100 lists methadone syrup, sublingual buprenorphine, buprenorphine-naloxone, and depot buprenorphine for OUD; the choice hinges on lifestyle, safety-critical work, home environment, and drug-drug interactions.

subtopic_detail: Buprenorphine micro-induction to avoid precipitated withdrawal
stem:
A 41-year-old woman on long-term methadone 80 mg daily for chronic pain from a spinal injury asks to transition to buprenorphine-naloxone because she is planning international travel and finds methadone dispensing arrangements impractical. She has been on methadone for 6 years. She takes it every morning under supervision and reports no illicit opioid use. Her most recent dose was 8 hours ago.

She has no other substance use, is not pregnant, has normal LFTs, no QT prolongation, and has read written information about the risks of switching. She strongly prefers not to experience any period of significant opioid withdrawal because she is the sole carer for her elderly father. Standard induction would require her to reach COWS >=12 before the first buprenorphine dose.

data_table.History: Methadone 80 mg daily x 6 years, no illicit use, no other substances
data_table.Reason for switch: Travel logistics, no illicit use, prefers no significant withdrawal window
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, QTc 410 ms, not pregnant
data_table.Preferences: Cannot tolerate a withdrawal window due to sole-carer responsibilities

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate induction approach?

options.text: Stop methadone, wait for COWS >=12 (typically 72 h), then buprenorphine 4 mg SL in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Standard induction from methadone requires 72-96 h wait and produces a substantial withdrawal window, which she cannot accommodate as sole carer. Micro-induction is the alternative (Source: RACGP MATOD).

options.text: Halve methadone to 40 mg for 3 days, then start buprenorphine 8 mg in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Simple methadone dose reduction does not lower the mu-agonist ceiling enough to avoid precipitated withdrawal at a buprenorphine 8 mg dose; risks the exact adverse event the patient wants to avoid (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

options.text: Give naloxone 0.4 mg IM before the first buprenorphine dose to shorten washout in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Precipitating a full antagonist reversal to shorten the switch is dangerous and not endorsed by any Australian guideline; it causes severe iatrogenic withdrawal (Source: AMH).

options.text: Switch directly to depot buprenorphine (Buvidal) at 24 mg SC without SL bridging in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Depot induction from methadone requires prior sublingual stabilisation or a micro-induction protocol; direct depot induction from a full agonist risks precipitated withdrawal and cannot be reversed until the depot dissipates (Source: RACGP MATOD).

options.text: Micro-induction: buprenorphine 0.5 mg SL day 1 while continuing methadone, doubling approximately every 1-2 days, stop methadone once buprenorphine reaches ~12 mg
options.rationale: The Bernese-style micro-induction (increasing sub-therapeutic buprenorphine while the full agonist remains on board) exploits buprenorphine's slow off-rate at the mu-opioid receptor to displace methadone gradually without a precipitated-withdrawal spike. AU addiction services increasingly offer this to patients who cannot tolerate a standard washout window. Once buprenorphine reaches approximately 8-12 mg daily, methadone can be stopped (Source: RACGP MATOD; AChAM position statement).
source_refs: AChAM Australasian Chapter of Addiction Medicine

explanation.summary: Micro-induction (Bernese method) allows transition from methadone to buprenorphine without a symptomatic withdrawal window by starting very-low-dose buprenorphine alongside continued full agonist and titrating up over days.
key_points: Standard induction: stop full agonist, wait COWS >=12 (72-96 h)
Micro-induction: overlap tiny buprenorphine doses with full agonist, double every 1-2 days
Rationale: buprenorphine slow off-rate at mu allows gradual displacement
Stop full agonist once buprenorphine ~8-12 mg
Depot buprenorphine requires prior SL stabilisation from full agonist
explanation.pearls: In context: micro-induction protocols are increasingly the AU standard for methadone-to-buprenorphine switching in patients who cannot afford a withdrawal window (parenting, working, chronic pain).

sources.label: AChAM Australasian Chapter of Addiction Medicine

subtopic_detail: Naltrexone vs acamprosate vs disulfiram - mechanism-based selection
stem:
A 46-year-old accountant attends her general practice in Perth requesting help to reduce her drinking. She currently drinks 6-8 standard drinks per evening, most days per week, describing the first drink as "the one I really look forward to". She has completed a supervised outpatient detoxification 4 weeks ago and has been abstinent since. Her goal is now sustained abstinence rather than controlled drinking.

She has no liver disease (LFTs and INR normal), is not on opioids for any indication, has never had opioid use disorder, has no seizure disorder, and is not planning pregnancy. She works in a client-facing role and is anxious about a medication that would make her acutely unwell if she "slipped" at a work function.

data_table.History: Detox 4 weeks ago, currently abstinent, wants sustained abstinence
data_table.Craving: Reports strong reward-response cravings, especially first drink of the evening
data_table.Investigations: LFTs and INR normal, U&E normal, not pregnant
data_table.Preferences: Prefers to avoid a drug that causes acute illness if she drinks

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Acamprosate 666 mg TDS orally in this scenario
options.rationale: Acamprosate is a glutamatergic modulator best suited to sustaining abstinence where protracted withdrawal and negative-reinforcement drinking predominate; would also be a reasonable second-line here but naltrexone matches her reward-craving phenotype better (Source: RACGP AUD).

options.text: Disulfiram 200 mg orally daily under supervision
options.rationale: Disulfiram produces an aversive reaction on drinking - she has expressly ruled this out; requires supervised administration and high adherence, less effective in unselected settings (Source: NHMRC).

options.text: Baclofen 10 mg TDS orally titrated in this scenario
options.rationale: Baclofen is a second- or third-line option in AUD, considered mainly when first-line agents are contraindicated (e.g. significant liver disease); not first-line here (Source: NHMRC).

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg orally daily in this scenario
options.rationale: Naltrexone is a mu-opioid antagonist that reduces the reward-response to alcohol; it is first-line where craving and reward drive drinking ("first drink is the best drink"). No opioid contraindication, no significant liver disease, and no aversive-reaction concern make it the best fit. AU listing on PBS is authority-required for AUD (Source: RACGP AUD guideline; AMH; NHMRC).

options.text: Topiramate 25 mg BD titrated in this scenario
options.rationale: Topiramate is off-label in AUD in AU and reserved as later-line; cognitive side effects can affect a client-facing role (Source: NHMRC).

explanation.summary: Naltrexone (mu-antagonist) suits reward-driven cravings; acamprosate (glutamatergic) suits maintenance abstinence with protracted withdrawal; disulfiram is aversive and requires supervision and adherence.
key_points: Naltrexone: reward-craving phenotype, no opioid use, no severe liver disease
Acamprosate: negative-reinforcement drinking, maintain abstinence
Disulfiram: aversive; requires supervision and adherence
Baclofen: reserved for severe liver disease or first-line failures
All AU AUD pharmacotherapies are PBS authority-required
explanation.pearls: In context: "first drink is the best drink" is a mnemonic for reward-craving that flags naltrexone; "drinking to feel normal" flags acamprosate.

subtopic_detail: IM sedation of acute methamphetamine intoxication
stem:
A 27-year-old man is brought into an outer-suburban Brisbane emergency department by paramedics after smashing furniture at a friend's house. He is dishevelled, sweating profusely, agitated, and shouting that people are watching him through the walls. He has confirmed methamphetamine use in the previous 12 hours. He refuses oral medication, cannot cooperate with venous access, and has been placed in a resuscitation cubicle with security in attendance.

He is 92 kg, has no known medical history, no known medications, and no known allergies. There is no evidence of trauma. Point-of-care glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. He is not sedated on inhaled agents. ECG is not yet feasible. Restraint is required for staff safety.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 168/98, RR 22, SpO2 97 percent, temp 38.4
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, agitated, paranoid, no focal neurology, no head injury
data_table.Access: No IV access; oral route refused
data_table.History: Confirmed methamphetamine use in prior 12 h; no other substances known

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first sedating agent?

options.text: Olanzapine 10 mg IM in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Olanzapine IM is a reasonable alternative but not first-line in AU stimulant intoxication guidelines; must not be combined with parenteral benzodiazepines within 60 min because of respiratory depression risk (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Midazolam 5 mg IM in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Midazolam alone is an alternative but has shorter duration and more respiratory depression risk; droperidol is preferred first-line in AU stimulant agitation (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.text: Haloperidol 5 mg IM plus promethazine 25 mg IM
options.rationale: Haloperidol-promethazine combination is a NICE regimen; AU practice favours droperidol monotherapy for stimulant agitation (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.text: Droperidol 10 mg IM in this clinical setting
options.rationale: AU acute behavioural disturbance guidelines (NSW MoH, Queensland Health) endorse droperidol 10 mg IM as first-line for severe stimulant-related agitation where IV access is not possible. Onset is 10-15 minutes and safety profile (including QT concerns) is well-characterised at this dose (Source: NSW Health Management of Patients with Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

options.text: Ketamine 4 mg/kg IM in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Ketamine is reserved for extreme agitation refractory to first-line droperidol/midazolam or where retrieval-medicine protocols apply; not first-line ward-ED practice (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

explanation.summary: AU acute severe behavioural disturbance guidelines recommend IM droperidol 10 mg as the first-line sedating agent for stimulant intoxication when IV access is not feasible.
key_points: Droperidol 10 mg IM first-line in AU for severe agitation
Olanzapine IM alternative, but avoid IM benzo within 60 min
Midazolam IM alternative but shorter and more respiratory depression
Ketamine reserved for refractory extreme cases
Physical monitoring: SpO2, HR, BP, temp every 15 min post-sedation
explanation.pearls: In context: rehydration, active cooling, and workup for rhabdomyolysis and hyponatraemia sit alongside sedation - agitation is only the presenting problem.

sources.label: NSW Health Acute Severe Behavioural Disturbance guideline

subtopic_detail: Meth-induced psychosis vs primary schizophrenia - course and antipsychotic pathway
stem:
A 24-year-old man is reviewed on the mental health unit after admission a week ago with paranoid delusions and auditory hallucinations. On admission urine drug screen was positive for methamphetamine and cannabis. He has been abstinent from all substances since admission (supervised, urine drug screens repeatedly negative). Over the last seven days his positive symptoms have improved substantially: he now denies paranoid content, sleeps normally, and is engaging in ward activities.

He has no family history of psychotic illness. He first used methamphetamine 3 years ago and has had two prior brief presentations with paranoid symptoms, each resolving within 1-2 weeks of abstinence. He is not on any regular medication. He was commenced on olanzapine 10 mg nocte on admission with good response.

data_table.History: Meth use 3 years, 2 prior brief paranoid episodes each resolved <2 weeks abstinence
data_table.Course this admission: Symptoms substantially resolved by day 7 abstinence on olanzapine 10 mg nocte
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative from day 2 onward; MSE now euthymic non-psychotic

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step for antipsychotic management?

options.text: Continue olanzapine 10 mg nocte lifelong and add a mood stabiliser in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Lifelong antipsychotic and mood stabiliser are not indicated for a clearly substance-induced psychotic episode with rapid resolution on abstinence (Source: RANZCP guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

options.text: Stop olanzapine tomorrow now symptoms have resolved in this clinical setting in accordance with department protocol
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after only 7 days risks relapse of positive symptoms during the vulnerable abstinence window; a staged taper over months is preferred (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Continue olanzapine for 3-6 months with staged taper, and refer to AOD service for relapse prevention
options.rationale: AU practice (RANZCP addiction faculty, eTG Psychotropic) for substance-induced psychosis that clearly resolves with abstinence is to continue the antipsychotic for 3-6 months while symptoms stabilise, then taper against ongoing abstinence, coupled with AOD engagement for relapse prevention. Prolonged empiric antipsychotic risks metabolic burden without benefit; premature cessation risks relapse and evolution to primary psychotic disorder (Source: RANZCP; eTG Psychotropic; RANZCP Addiction Faculty).

options.text: Switch to clozapine as evolving treatment-resistant schizophrenia in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Clozapine requires two documented antipsychotic failures at adequate dose/duration; the picture here is responsive substance-induced psychosis, not treatment resistance (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

options.text: Commence a long-acting injectable antipsychotic for improved adherence in this clinical setting
options.rationale: LAI is reserved for confirmed primary psychotic disorders with poor oral adherence; premature use in likely substance-induced psychosis is not supported (Source: RANZCP).
source_refs: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

explanation.summary: Methamphetamine-induced psychosis that resolves rapidly with abstinence is managed with 3-6 months of antipsychotic cover then staged taper, plus AOD relapse-prevention work; lifelong therapy is not indicated unless recurrence off substances occurs.
key_points: Substance-induced psychosis resolves within days-weeks of abstinence
Primary schizophrenia symptoms persist despite documented abstinence
3-6 months antipsychotic cover then staged taper is standard
AOD referral is core, not adjunctive
Recurrence off substances suggests primary psychotic disorder emerging
explanation.pearls: In context: 20-30 percent of meth-induced psychosis eventually converts to a primary psychotic disorder, so continued monitoring post-taper is essential.

sources.label: RANZCP Australian and New Zealand clinical practice guideline for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: GHB overdose - supportive monitoring, no reversal agent
stem:
A 22-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after collapsing at a Sydney nightclub. Her friend reports she took two capfuls of "G" approximately 45 minutes earlier and had a small amount of vodka. On arrival she is unresponsive to voice, groans to painful stimulus, and localises briefly. Her respiratory rate is 8 with normal SpO2 on 4 L nasal prongs and a preserved gag reflex. She is otherwise haemodynamically stable.

Capillary glucose is 4.8 mmol/L. Point-of-care venous blood gas: pH 7.32, pCO2 55 mmHg, bicarbonate 26 mmol/L. Urine drug screen for opioids and benzodiazepines is negative. There is no evidence of trauma. Paramedics have not given any medication.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 62, BP 108/68, RR 8, SpO2 98 percent on 4 L NP, temp 36.8
data_table.Examination: Preserved gag reflex, no head injury, no needle marks
data_table.Investigations: BSL 4.8, VBG pH 7.32 pCO2 55 HCO3 26, UDS opioid and benzo negative

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Supportive care in a monitored bed with continuous SpO2, capnography, and airway attendance until GCS returns to baseline
options.rationale: GHB overdose has no reversal agent. The mainstay is intensive supportive care in a monitored resuscitation bay with continuous SpO2 and capnography, airway attendance ready to intubate if apnoea or loss of gag develops, and observation until sedation resolves (typically within 2-4 hours). Do NOT give naloxone or flumazenil (no benefit, risk of confounding). Consider intubation only if apnoea, aspiration, or loss of airway reflexes (Source: eTG Toxicology; NSW Poisons Information Centre).

options.text: Naloxone 400 mcg IV bolus in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation
options.rationale: Naloxone does not reverse GHB (which acts via GABA-B and endogenous GHB receptors, not mu-opioid); no reversal agent exists (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Flumazenil 200 mcg IV bolus in this clinical setting as the primary intervention for this presentation under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses only benzodiazepines and carries seizure risk in undifferentiated overdose; not indicated for GHB (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation for airway protection in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: RSI is not automatically required at GCS 9 with a preserved gag and stable vitals; GHB coma typically resolves within 2-4 hours and premature intubation adds ventilator-associated risks (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Activated charcoal 50 g NG immediately in this clinical setting as the primary intervention and arrange next-day review
options.rationale: Charcoal in a patient with reduced GCS and no protected airway risks aspiration; GHB is also rapidly absorbed and decontamination is not effective 45 minutes post-ingestion (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: GHB overdose has no reversal agent; management is supportive with airway monitoring and observation for spontaneous emergence, typically within 2-4 hours. Intubate only if apnoea or loss of protective reflexes.
key_points: No reversal agent for GHB (GABA-B and specific GHB receptors)
Typical duration 2-4 hours
Airway attendance and capnography, not automatic intubation
Naloxone and flumazenil have no role and risk confounding
Screen for co-ingestants (ethanol, stimulants, benzos)
explanation.pearls: In context: patients often emerge suddenly and combatively from GHB coma - staff and equipment must be prepared for that transition.

subtopic_detail: MDMA hyponatraemia vs serotonin syndrome differentiation
stem:
A 19-year-old woman is brought to an emergency department in Adelaide by friends after collapsing with a generalised seizure at a music festival. She took MDMA approximately 6 hours ago. Her friends report she has been drinking large volumes of water throughout the day to "stay safe". On arrival she is post-ictal, confused, and has vomited once. There is no hyperreflexia, no ankle clonus, no ocular clonus, no muscle rigidity, and no severe hyperthermia.

Sodium is 118 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 3.2 mmol/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Urine osmolality is high relative to plasma osmolality. CK is 320 U/L. Serum tryptase, if it mattered, is not indicated. There is no other drug co-ingestion by history.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 122/78, RR 18, SpO2 98 percent, temp 37.6
data_table.Neuro: Post-ictal, no clonus, no rigidity, no hyperreflexia, no ocular clonus
data_table.Investigations: Na 118, K 3.6, urea 3.2, creatinine 62, glucose 5.4, CK 320

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Hypertonic (3 percent) saline 150 mL IV over 10 min, repeat once if seizure or persistent severe hyponatraemia
options.rationale: This is symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Na 118, seizure) caused by MDMA-induced SIADH plus large free-water intake. AU acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia guidance is 100-150 mL 3 percent saline IV over 10 min, repeated once if needed, aiming to raise Na by 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour to control seizure; total 24-hour rise capped at 10 mmol/L to avoid osmotic demyelination. Fluid restriction alone is inadequate when seizing (Source: eTG Endocrinology; eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Cyproheptadine 12 mg PO for serotonin syndrome in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Serotonin syndrome requires the triad of altered mental state, autonomic hyperactivity, and neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia, rigidity). She has none of the neuromuscular features - this is MDMA-induced hyponatraemia (SIADH), not serotonin syndrome (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Isotonic (0.9 percent) saline 1 L IV over 1 hour in this clinical setting as the primary intervention under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: In SIADH, isotonic saline can paradoxically worsen hyponatraemia because free water is retained while sodium is excreted; hypertonic saline is required for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

options.text: Fluid restriction to 800 mL/24 h with 6-hourly sodium recheck in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is chronic-SIADH management but is inadequate for acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with a seizure - hypertonic saline is required first (Source: eTG Endocrinology).

options.text: Dantrolene 2 mg/kg IV for suspected NMS variant in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia and severe NMS with hyperthermia and rigidity - neither is present here (Source: eTG Toxicology).

explanation.summary: MDMA-induced severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (Na 118, seizure) from SIADH plus water loading is treated with 3 percent saline boluses aiming to raise Na 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, capped at 10 mmol/L over 24 h. Serotonin syndrome requires neuromuscular hyperactivity that is absent here.
key_points: MDMA -> SIADH + intentional water loading -> hyponatraemia
Hypertonic saline for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia (Na <125 with seizure/coma)
Raise Na 4-6 mmol/L in first hour, cap at 10 mmol/L over 24 h
Serotonin syndrome triad: mental state, autonomic, neuromuscular
Isotonic saline worsens SIADH-driven hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: In context: young women are disproportionately affected because of smaller total body water and the SIADH effect of MDMA compounded by well-meaning water loading.

stem:
A 26-year-old plumber attends his general practice in regional Victoria asking for help to reduce his cannabis use. He has been smoking daily for 8 years, currently 3-5 cones each evening, and describes low motivation, disturbed sleep on the days he tries to abstain, and a growing worry about the impact on his work and relationship. He has no history of psychotic illness, no other substance use, no medical comorbidities, and no current suicidal ideation.

He has not tried any structured programme before. His partner is supportive and he wants to stop entirely.

data_table.History: Daily cannabis 8 years, 3-5 cones/evening, wants to stop entirely

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Naltrexone 50 mg PO daily in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Naltrexone has no established indication for cannabis use disorder (Source: AMH).

options.text: N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg BD PO in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine has mixed evidence in cannabis use disorder in adolescents; not first-line and not PBS-listed for this indication in AU (Source: AMH).

options.text: Prescribed dronabinol as a substitution therapy for this presentation under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Substitution therapy for cannabis is not an AU-approved treatment for cannabis use disorder outside research settings (Source: RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

options.text: Diazepam 5 mg PO nocte for 4 weeks for sleep and withdrawal under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are not indicated for cannabis withdrawal, carry dependence risk, and do not address the disorder (Source: eTG Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy and motivational interviewing under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Australian guidance (RACGP, National Cannabis Prevention and Information Centre, eTG) endorses CBT and motivational interviewing as first-line for cannabis use disorder. No pharmacotherapy is PBS-listed for cannabis use disorder; adjunctive short-term sleep advice and monitoring for withdrawal is standard (Source: RACGP; eTG Psychotropic).
source_refs: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

explanation.summary: Cannabis use disorder in AU is managed first-line with CBT and motivational interviewing; there is no PBS-listed pharmacotherapy.
key_points: CBT + MI is first-line
No PBS-listed pharmacotherapy for CUD in AU
Withdrawal peaks day 2-6, resolves ~2 weeks
Sleep advice and time-limited non-benzo sleep support if needed
Screen for co-occurring depression, anxiety, psychosis
explanation.pearls: In context: chronic high-potency THC use is a modifiable risk factor for psychotic illness in young adults - psychoeducation is part of care.

sources.label: RACGP guidance on cannabis use disorder

subtopic_detail: Benzodiazepine deprescribing via diazepam substitution taper
stem:
A 68-year-old woman has been on temazepam 20 mg nocte for insomnia for the last 12 years, initially started after her husband's death. She now wishes to stop because a family member had a fall after starting a similar medication. She has hypertension controlled on perindopril, no cognitive impairment on MoCA (28/30), no depression on PHQ-9, and no other sedative use. She lives independently, drives, and has no falls or fractures to date.

Renal function and LFTs are within normal limits. She has been counselled about withdrawal symptoms and the timeframe involved and is committed to a deliberate taper.

data_table.Medications: Temazepam 20 mg nocte x 12 years, perindopril, no other sedatives
data_table.Investigations: U&E and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate deprescribing approach?

options.text: Stop temazepam abruptly this week in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation after 12 years risks severe withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia rebound, seizures); tapering is required (Source: AMH; RACGP).

options.text: Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg nocte then taper over 4 weeks under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Zopiclone is not a taper-friendly substitute; it has its own dependence potential and swapping does not enable a smooth withdrawal (Source: AMH).

options.text: Add flumazenil 0.2 mg IV weekly to speed receptor down-regulation under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Flumazenil infusions for accelerated benzodiazepine detox are experimental, not AU standard, and carry seizure risk (Source: eTG Toxicology).

options.text: Add pregabalin 75 mg BD to cover withdrawal in this clinical setting under a supervising clinician
options.rationale: Pregabalin carries its own dependence and misuse risk in older adults; not routinely used to cover benzodiazepine withdrawal in AU (Source: AMH).

options.text: Convert to equivalent diazepam and reduce by 5-10 percent every 2 weeks in this scenario
options.rationale: AU deprescribing guidance (RACGP; NSW Health) is to substitute the short/intermediate-acting benzodiazepine (temazepam 20 mg ~= diazepam 10 mg) with equivalent diazepam and reduce by 5-10 percent of the starting dose every 1-2 weeks, slower toward the end. Diazepam's long half-life smooths withdrawal. Non-pharmacological insomnia strategies (CBT-I) are co-delivered (Source: RACGP; NSW Health).

explanation.summary: Long-term benzodiazepine deprescribing uses equivalent-dose diazepam substitution and slow taper (5-10 percent every 1-2 weeks) alongside CBT-I; abrupt cessation risks seizures.
key_points: Temazepam 20 mg ~= diazepam 10 mg
Reduce by 5-10 percent every 1-2 weeks, slower at the end
Diazepam long half-life smooths withdrawal
CBT-I is core alongside pharmacological taper
Never abrupt-stop after prolonged use - seizure risk
explanation.pearls: In context: elderly women on long-term benzodiazepines are a common deprescribing cohort; falls, cognitive impairment and MVA risk make sustained withdrawal worthwhile.

stem:
A 39-year-old man attends his general practice in Perth requesting a mental health care plan for "anxiety". On further discussion he tells you he has been staying up late at night placing bets on international sport, is now taking cash advances from his credit card to keep betting, and hides his gambling from his partner. He denies any substance use, has never attempted suicide, and has no other psychiatric history. He is asking for help.

He is otherwise well, on no medications, and has never been assessed for gambling before. You want to briefly screen for gambling disorder in the consultation before proceeding to a more detailed assessment.

data_table.History: Escalating sports betting, credit-card cash advances, concealing from partner
data_table.Prior assessment: Never screened or assessed for gambling

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate brief screening tool?

options.text: PHQ-9 depression screen in this scenario
options.rationale: PHQ-9 screens for depression, not gambling; useful adjunct but not the primary tool here (Source: RACGP).

options.text: Lie/Bet screen (two questions)
options.rationale: The Lie/Bet screen is a validated 2-item screen for problem gambling that AU primary care resources (RACGP, Gambling Help Online) recommend as the first-pass tool: (1) Have you ever lied to people important to you about how much you gambled? (2) Have you ever felt the need to bet more and more money? A yes to either warrants full assessment (e.g. PGSI) (Source: RACGP; Gambling Help Online).

options.text: AUDIT-C alcohol screen in this scenario
options.rationale: AUDIT-C is an alcohol tool; useful comorbidity screen, not primary here (Source: RACGP).

options.text: K10 psychological distress screen
options.rationale: K10 measures nonspecific psychological distress; complements but does not replace a gambling-specific screen (Source: RACGP).

options.text: GAD-7 anxiety screen in this scenario
options.rationale: GAD-7 measures anxiety severity; will not identify gambling disorder (Source: RACGP).

explanation.summary: Lie/Bet is the recommended 2-item brief screen for problem gambling in AU primary care; a positive answer to either question prompts full assessment (e.g. PGSI, DSM-5-TR criteria).
key_points: Lie/Bet: 2 items, positive on either -> full assessment
PGSI (9 items) for severity classification
Naltrexone has some evidence in gambling disorder (off-label)
First-line management is psychological therapy (CBT)
Screen for depression, alcohol use disorder, suicidality co-occurrence
explanation.pearls: In context: gambling disorder is a DSM-5-TR behavioural addiction that clusters with substance use disorders, depression, and suicide - screening the cluster together is efficient.

stem:
A 33-year-old man presents to a public drug and alcohol inpatient unit in Melbourne requesting supervised withdrawal. He drinks 18 standard drinks daily, uses diazepam 40 mg daily (obtained from multiple prescribers), and uses methamphetamine intranasally 3-4 times per week. He has no cardiac history and has previously had one alcohol withdrawal seizure. He is committed to abstinence and has arranged accommodation and residential rehabilitation for after detox.

He has no active infection, LFTs are mildly elevated (ALT 65, AST 55), INR 1.1, and no signs of hepatic encephalopathy. Renal function and electrolytes are within normal limits. He is not currently intoxicated on arrival.

data_table.Substances: Alcohol 18 SD/day, diazepam 40 mg/day, meth 3-4x/week intranasal
data_table.History: Prior alcohol withdrawal seizure, wants abstinence, rehab arranged
data_table.Investigations: ALT 65, AST 55, INR 1.1, UEC within normal limits

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate detoxification sequencing plan?

options.text: Complete meth detox first, then alcohol, then benzodiazepine in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Meth has no physiological withdrawal syndrome requiring pharmacological detox; sequencing alcohol/benzodiazepine after "meth detox" wastes time and delays the highest-risk withdrawal (Source: eTG Addiction).

options.text: Alcohol first with diazepam, discharge, and re-admit for benzodiazepine detox in 3 months in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Splitting cross-tolerant GABAergic detox across admissions risks rebound and undermines the planned rehab pathway; parallel management is preferred (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Detox benzodiazepine over 6 months as outpatient before admission for alcohol detox in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Ongoing heavy alcohol use during a 6-month outpatient benzo taper is high risk and does not accomplish the goal of a single supervised withdrawal (Source: NSW Health).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Detox alcohol and benzodiazepine simultaneously with symptom-triggered diazepam CIWA-guided, then meth psychosocial support
options.rationale: Alcohol and benzodiazepine both act at GABA-A; they are managed in parallel with a single diazepam-based taper that first covers alcohol withdrawal symptoms (CIWA-Ar) and then transitions to a scheduled diazepam taper for the benzodiazepine component. Methamphetamine does not have a physiological withdrawal syndrome needing pharmacotherapy; psychosocial support (motivational interviewing, sleep hygiene) is the mainstay. Prior withdrawal seizure raises the priority for effective GABAergic cover (Source: NSW Health D and A Withdrawal; eTG Addiction).
source_refs: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

options.text: Refuse admission until meth is stopped for 4 weeks in this clinical setting as the primary intervention
options.rationale: Requiring pre-abstinence to access a supervised withdrawal service is not AU practice and creates unnecessary access barriers (Source: eTG Addiction).

explanation.summary: Alcohol and benzodiazepine (both GABA-A) detoxes are managed in parallel with a single diazepam-based regimen; meth needs psychosocial support, not pharmacological detox.
key_points: Alcohol + benzo = single GABAergic detox with diazepam
Meth has no pharmacological detox pathway (dopaminergic, not GABA)
CIWA-Ar covers alcohol component; scheduled diazepam covers benzo taper
Rehab handoff post-detox is core, not optional
Splitting cross-tolerant detoxes across admissions is unsafe
explanation.pearls: In context: identifying which of a patient's substances actually have physiological withdrawal (alcohol, benzos, opioids, GHB) versus psychological withdrawal (cocaine, methamphetamine, cannabis) drives the sequencing.

sources.label: NSW Health Drug and Alcohol Withdrawal Clinical Practice Guidelines

stem:
A 29-year-old woman at 14 weeks gestation attends a specialist drug and alcohol clinic in Sydney for review of her opioid use. She has been on methadone 60 mg daily for two years and is stable, working part-time, and engaged with antenatal care. She has read online that methadone crosses the placenta and asks whether she should stop it now, taper it, or switch to buprenorphine or buprenorphine-naloxone for the rest of the pregnancy.

She has no other substance use (urine drug screens negative for other opioids, benzodiazepines, meth), no infection, and LFTs are normal. She is not on any other CNS depressants. She has no history of opioid diversion, has children in the home from a previous relationship, and asks specifically about the safest option for her baby.

data_table.History: Methadone 60 mg daily x 2 years, stable, working, engaged in antenatal care
data_table.Investigations: UDS negative for other substances, LFTs normal, no infection
data_table.Home: Children from prior relationship in the home

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate opioid-use management plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Continue methadone at current stable dose; monitor for dose adjustments as pregnancy progresses
options.rationale: AU guidance (National Guidelines for MATOD, RANZCOG) is that stable methadone is continued at the effective dose during pregnancy, with dose adjustments (often split-dosing or dose increases in the third trimester) as metabolism accelerates. Switching stable methadone to buprenorphine-naloxone antenatally is not routinely done because of switching-related destabilisation risk. Buprenorphine (mono-product) is preferred over buprenorphine-naloxone in pregnancy where a NEW start is planned. NAS is managed at delivery with the neonatal team (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RANZCOG).

options.text: Taper methadone off during the second trimester in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Tapering opioid substitution off during pregnancy is not recommended - it carries relapse and overdose risk that far exceeds any theoretical benefit of avoiding neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS). Continue maintenance (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD; RANZCOG).

options.text: Switch to buprenorphine-naloxone 8 mg/2 mg daily this trimester in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Switching a stable pregnant patient off methadone risks destabilisation; if a switch is chosen, mono-buprenorphine (not the naloxone-combined product) is the AU-preferred pregnancy product (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

options.text: Cease methadone at 36 weeks to avoid neonatal abstinence syndrome in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Late-pregnancy cessation is associated with relapse and preterm delivery risk; maintenance continued to delivery with neonatal team preparation is standard (Source: RANZCOG).

options.text: Start naltrexone after supervised detox for the third trimester in this clinical setting
options.rationale: Naltrexone maintenance in pregnancy is not AU-standard and detoxification during pregnancy is high-risk; maintenance is preferred (Source: National Guidelines for MATOD).

explanation.summary: Stable opioid substitution in pregnancy is continued (not tapered), with dose adjustment as pregnancy metabolism accelerates and neonatal team involvement for NAS at delivery. Switching stable methadone antenatally is not routine.
key_points: Continue stable methadone through pregnancy; anticipate 3rd trimester dose increase or split dosing
Buprenorphine mono-product preferred over combo in pregnancy
Do NOT taper off maintenance antenatally - relapse and overdose risk
NAS prepared for at delivery, not prevented by ceasing maintenance
Breastfeeding compatible with methadone and buprenorphine
explanation.pearls: In context: benzodiazepine co-use in pregnancy is separately deprescribed via slow diazepam taper, alcohol is abstinence, and stimulant co-use is managed psychosocially - each substance in a polysubstance-using pregnant woman needs its own plan.

stem: A 44-year-old woman attends her general practice for a routine review. She reports drinking approximately 5 standard drinks on a Friday and 5 standard drinks on a Saturday, with no drinking on other days. She has no medical comorbidities, is not pregnant, is not on any medication, and has no personal or family history of substance use disorder. She asks whether her current drinking pattern is within the recommended Australian guidelines.

data_table.History: 10 SD/week, split as 5 Friday + 5 Saturday; no other drinking days

lead_in: What is the single most accurate answer per the NHMRC 2020 Australian alcohol guidelines?

options.text: Both weekly and per-session amounts breach the guideline
options.rationale: Weekly total of 10 SD sits at the cap, not above it; only per-session limit is breached (Source: NHMRC 2020).

options.text: Her weekly total is within the guideline but per-session amount exceeds it
options.rationale: The NHMRC 2020 Australian guidelines to reduce health risks from drinking alcohol recommend healthy adults drink no more than 10 standard drinks per week AND no more than 4 standard drinks on any one day. Her weekly total (10) sits at the cap, but 5 drinks in one session breaches the single-session limit (Source: NHMRC 2020).

options.text: Both weekly and per-session amounts are within the guideline
options.rationale: Per-session limit is 4 SD; 5 SD per session exceeds it (Source: NHMRC 2020).

options.text: Weekly amount breaches guideline, per-session amount is within
options.rationale: Weekly limit is 10 SD; her total sits at the cap; per-session is the breach (Source: NHMRC 2020).

options.text: The guideline uses total weekly ethanol grams, not standard drinks
options.rationale: The NHMRC guideline is expressed in Australian standard drinks (10 g ethanol per standard drink), not grams (Source: NHMRC 2020).

explanation.summary: NHMRC 2020 alcohol guidelines: healthy adults no more than 10 standard drinks per week AND no more than 4 on any one day; pregnancy and under-18 = zero.
key_points: 10 SD/week AND 4 SD/session for healthy adults
Pregnancy: no alcohol
Under 18: no alcohol
1 AU standard drink = 10 g ethanol
Guidelines are population risk-reduction, not safe-use thresholds
explanation.pearls: In context: brief interventions in general practice for above-guideline drinkers deliver measurable reductions and are AU-funded via the mental health care plan / chronic disease framework.
